Sudden MM inventory shocks on HYPE

When a market maker's inventory changes suddenly and by a lot, what caused it, who else was affected, and how does the MM get out — measured against the whole active market-maker population, not one MM.

Shocks detected181
Sample window2025-03-27 → 2026-06-30
Detection population10 top-volume HYPE MMs
Comparison populationAll labeled HYPE MMs
Exposure3,198 active wallet-days
Shock rate5.66 per 100 active wallet-days
Detector precision92.2% (64 panels audited)
Evidence typeDescriptive, not causal
Interpretation boundary. Everything here is a descriptive association measured on a five-minute grid. "A taker surge caused the shock" means a flow burst and an inventory build occupied the same ten minutes — nothing stronger. Shocks are detected on ten wallets only, so shock counts and rates describe those ten; every cross-sectional comparison is against the full MM population.

Overview: the two studies and what they found

The same ten HYPE market-maker MMs, the same fifteen months, and two deliberately different definitions of a sudden inventory event. Exp5 splits events by whether the position comes back — excursions that revert (spikes) against step changes that stay (cliffs). Exp8 asks only whether the move was sudden and large, and records what followed as a label. This section is what both found and the evidence behind it; sections A–F are Exp8 in full, and Exp5 has its own report.

The four things to take away. (1) The same ten HYPE market-maker wallets produce two distinct kinds of sudden inventory event — excursions that come back, and step changes that stay — and which kind an MM produces is a property of the MM, not of how much inventory it moves. (2) The events that come back are one-sided taker bursts absorbed on resting quotes, and they are absorbed by many MMs at once — never one. (3) Absorbing a burst and keeping it are different things: absorbing MMs hand back about 43 of every 100 HYPE they buy by the time the shock peaks, and getting the rest off takes hours — the median shocked MM still carries 38% of its excursion six hours later. (4) Nothing here is causal, and nothing here says the MMs trade badly: benchmarked against every other market maker trading the same side at the same moment, the shocked MM's execution is a coin flip.

Scope: what each study covers

Exp5 — spikes and cliffsExp8 — shocks
Question When an MM's inventory jumps within a day, does it come back? What do the two cases look like? When it jumps suddenly, what caused it, who else was hit, and how does the MM get out?
Detected on The same fixed roster of ten top-volume dominant HYPE market-maker wallets (the Exp7 roster; no new label join in either experiment).
Compared against The same ten. A separate scan covers 263 wallets, for rates only. Every wallet labeled a HYPE MM on the event date — a median 249 labeled, of which 95 clear the pre-event activity gate.
Window2025-03-27 → 2026-06-30 UTC, identical in both.
Exposure (the denominator) 3,198 active wallet-days — a date on which the wallet made ≥300 grouped fills and traded ≥$1m. Same screen in both, so the rates are comparable.
What is measured on The wallet's HYPE position in five-minute bins, rebuilt from its own fills, minus its trailing six-hour rolling median — divided by the wallet's own trailing robust scale σ (exact equations directly below this table). Every MM is judged against itself.
What counts as an event Spike: ≥8× the wallet's own normal deviation, ≥$100k, peak reached within 25 minutes, and it returns — retraces at least half, comes back through a narrow band on both sides, and leaves no lasting level change.
Cliff: the mirror image — a 5-to-60-minute one-way move of ≥6× the wallet's own scale, with ≥70% of it still there one hour and two hours later.		 Shock: ≥6× the wallet's own normal deviation measured on a trailing 7-day scale, ≥$100k, with 60% of the build inside a single 25-minute stretch, and standing out 1.5× from its neighbours on both sides. Whether it comes back is not part of the rule — it is recorded afterwards as a label (revert / partial / step).
Events found 107 spikes and 168 cliffs 181 shocks (125 up, 56 down)
Rate 3.35 spikes and 5.25 cliffs per 100 active wallet-days 5.66 shocks per 100 active wallet-days
How precision was established Panels read one at a time, one verdict each, across five detector versions: ~95% of spikes and 97.6% of cliffs judged genuine (164 true, 1 drift, 3 ambiguous, 0 mislabelled spikes). Same instrument: 92.2% — 59 true of 64 panels, drawn at random in two independent draws (40 at one seed, 24 at another).
Per-fill attribution available Yes for spikes — flow, execution, markouts. None at all for cliffs. Yes — population absorption, unwind paths, peer-benchmarked execution, and exact counterparty pairing (the latter only up to 2025-11-24).
Kind of evidence Descriptive association on a five-minute grid. Neither experiment establishes cause.

The exact construction

For one wallet at five-minute bin t (all quantities are per-wallet), with position Pt in HYPE and mid price mt:

devt  =  Pt − median(Pt−72, …, Pt−1) trailing 6-hour median: 72 bins, ≥36 valid — centers the position at the wallet's own current level

σ7dt  =  1.4826 × median( |devs| : s an active-day bin in the trailing 7 days ) 2,016 bins, ≥288 valid — a robust (MAD) spread of the deviation; sets the unit

σt  =  max( σ7dt,  0.02 × p95(|P|)30d,  $12,500 / mt ) p95 of |position| over the trailing 30 days, lagged one day so it never sees the shock

zt  =  devt / σt ,   shock candidate when |zt| ≥ 6

So z is a robust z-score — median/MAD, not mean/standard-deviation — with two floors on the denominator: the p95 term keeps a wallet that has been unusually flat for a week from generating shocks out of noise, and the $12,500 floor does the same for small books. The constants are not free parameters: $12,500 = $100k / (z = 6), rounded down — since detection needs a move of 6σ and σ can never fall below the floor, the floor implies a minimum move of 6 × $12.5k = $75k, kept deliberately below the explicit $100k size gate so the floor only prevents division by a near-zero MAD and never becomes a second size rule. c = 0.02 removes 2 of 183 candidate events, both from the one wallet whose MAD collapses to ~1.8% of its own p95 position; c = 0.05 would remove 12 (sensitivity: tables/scale_floor_impact.csv). The two windows do different jobs and coexist inside the same z: the 6-hour median centers (what is this wallet's level right now), the 7-day MAD scales (what is a normal-sized wobble for it). Neither replaced the other at any point. A 12-hour centering window is run alongside as a robustness variant (132 shocks vs 181; section B). Exp5 differs only in using one full-sample scale per wallet instead of the trailing σ7dt.

Equity and effective leverage around each shock. Leverage is measured per fill: lev = k × 2 × max leverage, where k = maintenance margin / pool equity from the per-fill k dataset and HYPE's max leverage is 10 throughout the sample — so liquidation sits at 20× (k = 1); exact at the base maintenance tier.   • The typical shock does not dent equity. The median change is +0.06% from pre to after-peak and +0.07% to after +6 h; equity falls in only 47.8% / 43.8% / 49.3% of shocks (pre→after-peak / after-peak→+6h / pre→+6h) — a coin flip. The mean is −1.8%: a small tail of shocks loses percent-level equity while the median shock loses nothing.
  • Leverage rises into the peak more often than not (66.3% of shocks) but by a negligible amount (median Δ +0.02×, p75 +0.09×). The stronger fact is selection: during shock windows effective leverage runs at 2.3× its all-times median (0.65× vs 0.28×) — shocks happen when MMs are already running more levered — yet even the in-shock p75 (1.68×) sits a factor of twelve from the 20× liquidation boundary.
  • Coverage: equity 151 / 141 / 154 of 181 at the three reference points (checkpoint gaps and the 2025-11-20→28 panel hole); leverage 95 / 97 / 90 of the 99 leverage-era shocks.
  • A — exposure = |position| valued at the bin-open mid, so long and short bins do not cancel; ALL active-day bins (919,081 wallet-bins across the 3,198 wallet-days), not shock windows. Per-MM panels in A1.
  • B — devt/σt exactly as defined above, floors included: the same z the detector thresholds at 6.
  • C — the 181 catalogued shocks. |deviation| at peak = the position's distance from its trailing 6-hour median at the peak bin — i.e. how far the position stands above (or below) its own pre-shock level, in dollars at the concurrent mid.
  • D — whole-market taker imbalance (buy−sell)/(buy+sell) per 5-minute bin, 132,333 bins.
  • E — exchange-reported account value, last snapshot per UTC day. Coverage 2025-09-27 → 2026-06-30 only (99 of the 181 shocks fall inside it), snapshot cadence ~2 h in 2025 degrading to ~5.5 h by mid-2026. Zero-value snapshots are exchange-reported (emptied accounts), kept as recorded.

Both catalogues are frozen, and both precision figures are counts of human verdicts on rendered panels, not estimates from a model. That is the reason to trust the event lists at all.

What Exp5 observed: two families of event

  • Two families of event, and they sort the MMs. A spike reverts; a cliff stays. Ranks 6 and 8 produce zero spikes and 34 cliffs between them; ranks 2, 7 and 10 produce 54 spikes and 1 cliff; rank 1 does both (28 spikes, 97 cliffs). Rates over the same 3,198 active wallet-days (Exp5 §E). In the wider cohort of 263 dominant-MM wallets: 4.34 spikes and 8.33 cliffs per 100 wallet-days, and 49% of wallets produce neither (Exp5 §F).
  • A spike is absorbed flow, later unwound. Many takers converge on one side within a few minutes, the MM takes the other side on resting quotes, and the position is worked back to its level (Exp5 §C1).
  • The cost is in the move that follows. Volume-weighted maker markout 60 minutes out: −1.41 bps on spike-window fills against +1.73 bps on the same wallets' other fills that day (both excluding 2025-10-10, which alone is −118.53 bps); up-spikes +2.50, down-spikes −9.08. An earlier positive estimate was an artifact of a 25-minute build cap and is corrected in Exp5 §C3.
  • A cliff is a re-targeted book. Median $1.54m moved in 50 minutes and kept; 72 of 168 flip the sign of the position outright; 105 up, 63 down (Exp5 §D).

What Exp8 observed: cause, absorption, unwind

  • A shock is a one-sided taker burst, not a busy market. Over the 181 shocks, taker volume on the side trading against the MM runs at a median 5.29× its trailing 24-hour rate; some hit-side surge is present in 92.8% of shocks and exceeds 2× in 82.9%; taker imbalance toward that side is +0.443 and the flow is one-sided in 87.8%. Both sides accelerate — in the three episodes measured minute by minute the hit side runs 6.4× / 27.3× / 60.3× against 3.7× / 14.0× / 34.3× for total volume — — everything sped up, and the side hitting the MM sped up far more (§C).
  • Takers sell into these MMs about twice as often as they buy. 125 up shocks against 56 down (§C).
  • No shock is absorbed alone. The gross flow on the shock side is as concentrated as 11.3 equal MMs in the median shock (p5 5.2, p95 20.1; the most concentrated single case in the whole catalogue is 1.06), spread over a median of 71 absorbing wallets out of 95 active. The denominator decides this: over the ten roster wallets only the shocked MM holds 60–77% of same-side movement, but against every active MM the largest single MM holds 23–36% and the ten together 36–47%. "It absorbed this alone" is what a ten-wallet denominator looks like (§D).
  • Absorbing a shock and keeping it are different things. Same wallets, same fills, same window, same unit: gross buying is as concentrated as 11.3 equal MMs, what those MMs still hold at the peak as 7.4 — a per-shock ratio of 1.47, above 1 in 93% of shocks. The entire gap is round-tripping: widening the population changes it by −0.02 and reading the position off the panel instead of the fills by +0.01 (§D1).
  • Absorbing MMs keep a median 57 of every 100 HYPE they buy, and the distribution is split, not centred: 25% of absorbing MMs keep 10% or less of what they took, 37% keep 90% or more. Keeping falls with size: 0.82 in the smallest size quintile against 0.44 in the largest. In the median shock the absorbers buy 248,700 HYPE ($9.86m at the peak mid) on the shock side and are still holding 145,100 HYPE ($5.61m) of it at the peak. Evidence: 13,925 shock × wallet rows (§D1).
  • Why the shocked MM is the one left holding it: it recycles less, not that it caught more. Most MMs that absorb a burst sell much of it straight back out inside the same window. Of every 100 HYPE bought on the shock side, the median absorber is still holding 57 at the peak — and the biggest absorbers hold the least (44 per 100 in the largest size quintile, against 82 in the smallest), because size and re-offloading go together. The shocked MM is one of the largest absorbers in almost every event (97.8th percentile), so on size alone it should be among the heaviest re-offloaders. It is not: it holds about 11 more HYPE per 100 than MMs that absorbed a similar amount in the same event (paired median +0.112, positive in 63% of 161 shocks, Wilcoxon p = 3e‑08). The comparison is against similar-sized absorbers deliberately — against the average small absorber the gap would just be measuring size. The gap is widest exactly where it should be, on shocks whose position never comes back (+0.228 for step, +0.031 for revert). An earlier draft's "holds roughly twice the share it absorbed" is retracted: like for like the per-shock ratio is 1.19, and below 1 in 28% of shocks (§D1).
  • Most shocked MMs are outside the detected ten. In the three detailed episodes, 9 of 13, 10 of 13 and 26 of 31 MMs hit for 3× their own scale were not roster members. Shocked MMs are almost always shocked on the same side as the event; the crash day is the exception — 10 of 41 were shocked the other way, a two-sided cascade (§D2).
  • Getting out is slow and often incomplete. Aligning every shocked MM on its own peak and scaling by its own excursion: the median still carries 38% of it six hours later, only 61% ever get three-quarters back, and the 75th-percentile path sits at exactly 1.00 for the full six hours — a quarter of shocked MMs simply keep the position. Shocked MMs outside the ten are slower still (median 0.56 at six hours), so reading recovery speed off ten large MMs overstates how fast this population gets flat (§E1).
  • Execution during the unwind is unremarkable, and that is a finding. Every number here is benchmarked against every MM trading the same side, in the same 60 minutes, off the same reference price.
    • Price against its own peak mid: +16.2 bps; peer median +18.3.
    • 30-minute markout: −7.6 bps; peer median −8.8.
    • 60-minute markout: −15.3 bps; peer median −10.7.
    • Like for like, the gap is 0.4 bp on price and 1.0 bp on both markouts, putting the shocked MM at the 46th to 49th percentile of its peers. Those gaps are medians of the per-shock paired difference, so by construction they are not the difference of the two medians listed above.
    • A negative markout is the normal condition here, not a symptom: that side of that window paid everybody.
    • MMs that got flat fast printed far worse absolute prices, −76.9 bps against the peak mid versus +14.1 bps for MMs that sat still. Benchmarked, what separates them is when they traded, not how well (§E2).
  • Unwinding is a post-only activity. Across the 181 shocks the ten MMs unwind with post-only limit orders (84.4% of volume on average, 97.9% median) and immediate-or-cancel orders (14.3% average) — 98.7% together, and not once with a scheduled time-weighted order or a frontend market order. Two of the ten are exceptions and cross the spread routinely (one for 80% of its unwind volume). The concession is in where quotes sit, not in crossing the spread (§E2).
  • Market makers are a large share of each other's flow. From exact counterparty pairing, when an MM crosses the spread during these events 20.9% / 41.1% / 64.2% of that volume is taken from another MM's resting quote across the three episodes. Shocked-MM-to-shocked-MM volume is negligible in normal conditions ($0.08m) and $2.10m on the crash day — under stress they do unload into each other, though the data cannot separate that from "peers were simply the resting liquidity" (§D3).

The figure behind these numbers is below at full size: Figure 7, how a shocked MM's inventory comes back, as quantile bands on event time.

Why there are two catalogues, and how they overlap

The two definitions are deliberately different, and the catalogues overlap without either containing the other. At its operating threshold Exp8 keeps 55.1% of Exp5's 107 spikes and 18.5% of its 168 cliffs. Three reasons, all mechanical:

  • The yardstick changed, which matters more than the threshold number looks. Exp8 measures each move against the wallet's trailing seven-day scale, and that scale runs about 1.8× the full-sample scale precisely at event times. So Exp8's "6×" is a stricter test than Exp5's "8×", despite the smaller number.
  • Most cliffs fail the suddenness rule. 46% of cliffs sit exactly at Exp5's 60-minute ceiling, and a 60-minute one-way move can place at most about 42% of itself inside any 25-minute stretch, against Exp8's 60% requirement.
  • Exp8 refuses to put the outcome in the definition. Its step class is conceptually a cliff and its revert class conceptually a spike; it labels what happened afterwards instead of gating on it. Exp5 asks "did the MM absorb and return, or re-target?", which needs the outcome in the rule; Exp8 asks "how often does inventory move suddenly, whatever follows?", which needs it out. Neither framing is more correct.

What neither study establishes

Both studies are descriptive. What follows bounds what can be said from them; §F carries Exp8's full list, including its two known data defects.

  • Nothing is causal. A taker burst and an inventory build occupying the same ten minutes is an association on a five-minute grid, not a demonstrated cause.
  • Detection is on ten wallets in both studies. Events where only other market makers were hit are invisible, and there are no event counts or rates for anyone outside the ten: Exp5's 263-wallet scan gives rates only, and Exp8's population work is all measured inside windows the ten defined.
  • Counts are concentrated in a few MMs. Rank 2 is 41 of 107 spikes; rank 1 is 97 of 168 cliffs; two wallets are 99 of 181 shocks and three contribute 6 between them. Any per-wallet cell in single digits is indicative only.
  • Precision is 92–98%, not 100%, and the residual failures are recorded rather than tuned away: small events in wallets that oscillate constantly, and events whose peak sits hours after the fast move.
  • Quoting is only observed where a quote was filled. There is no order-lifecycle data, so nothing here describes posted quote distance, quoted size or a MM's own bid–ask spread. Every "spread" figure is a realized, fill-conditional price gap.
  • Cliffs have no attribution at all. Whether they are informed repositioning or forced unwinding is untested — the obvious next experiment.
  • 2025-10-10 is a distinct regime — 41% of its formation flow is forced liquidation or auto-deleveraging, and markout magnitudes are an order of magnitude larger. It is reported separately throughout and must not be pooled.
  • Slow permanent re-targeting is out of scope by construction in both detectors. An MM that moves inventory slowly registers zero events, and one of the ten does exactly that. Zero means "no sudden change", never "no inventory change".

If the slot is 20 minutes rather than 15, the two places worth the extra time are the D1 ladder (why one number was compared with another it should never have been compared with, and what the like-for-like answer is) and G4 (why two catalogues exist at all). Neither needs a new figure.

A. Definitions

Every term used later, defined once. Positions are sizes in HYPE; money amounts name their valuation price.

Inventory (position)
The wallet's signed HYPE position: positive = long. Sampled at the end of each five-minute bin, so the change across a bin equals that bin's net signed fills.
Deviation
Position minus the wallet's own trailing six-hour rolling median position. This is the quantity a shock is measured on — not the raw position level.
Trailing scale (σ)
How much this wallet's deviation normally moves, computed as a robust spread of its own recent deviations, floored so a temporarily quiet wallet cannot get an artificially tiny scale. Each wallet is judged against itself.
z
Deviation divided by that wallet's trailing scale. z = 6 means "six times this wallet's own normal deviation".
Formation window
The tightest interval ending at the deviation peak that contains 80% of the build-up. All cause-side measurement uses this, not the wider detection window. Median length 10 minutes.
Hit side
The taker side trading against the MM. MM inventory up means takers were selling to it; inventory down means takers were buying from it.
Opposite side
The other taker side. Reported separately because "all trading surged" and "the side that hit the MM surged" are different claims.
Surge ratio
Volume rate during formation divided by that same rate's trailing median. Computed separately for total, hit-side and opposite-side volume.
Active MM
A wallet labeled a HYPE market maker on that date that was genuinely trading just before the event: at least 10 grouped fills and volume above a measured floor in the prior two hours. This count is the denominator of every share below.
Shocked MM
An active MM whose inventory change over the event window exceeds 3× its own trailing scale. Judged in either direction, so "were they on the same side?" is a question and not an assumption.
Absorption
Maker fills on the shock side during formation — who supplied the liquidity the takers consumed. Gross: every such fill counts, with no netting against what the wallet sold back.
Retention
Size in HYPE still held at the peak divided by the gross size it bought on the shock side in the same window — HYPE over HYPE, same wallet, same window. 1 means it kept everything it took; 0 means it passed all of it straight back out.
Effective number of participants
1 / Σ share² over a stated participant set: the number of equal-sized participants that would give the same concentration. Not a count of wallets — 71 wallets with an effective N of 11 means their flow was as concentrated as 11 equal MMs splitting all of it. Lower = more concentrated. Being an index over one participant set, it is not comparable across two different sets.
Remaining shock fraction
Used for unwind paths. 1 at the wallet's own peak, 0 when the position is back to where it was when the window opened. Above 1 = the position kept growing; below 0 = overshoot past the starting level.
Markout M5 / M30 / M60
Signed profit on a fill measured against the midpoint 5, 30 or 60 minutes later. Positive = favorable to the wallet. Reported volume-weighted in basis points.
Price versus peak mid
The volume-weighted price of the wallet's shock-reducing fills against the midpoint at its own peak, signed so positive = better than flattening instantly at the peak.
Peer gap and percentile
The focal wallet's metric minus the median of other wallets trading the same side in the same window, and its rank among them (50 = typical, 0 = worst).
Shock class
Whether the position came back: revert (returns to its prior level), step (stays at the new level), partial (in between). An outcome label, never part of the detection rule.
Roster rank
Identity only: rank 1 is the highest-lifetime-volume MM of the ten. Not a performance or within-event ranking.

B. What counts as a shock

A shock is a sudden, large inventory change. Whether the MM gets the inventory back is a measured outcome, not part of the definition — so both reverting excursions and permanent level changes qualify.

B1. What we tried, and what it cost

Two detector versions were built and every detected panel was read by an independent reviewer before any downstream statistic was trusted.

  • Version 1 — 82.5% of panels judged genuine. Two failure modes: long merged windows that stitched several moves together, and small wave-like wiggles in permanently choppy wallets.
  • A defect in the speed test itself. Version 1 measured "how fast did this build?" across the whole window. For a one-bin spike, any window containing the peak also contains the reversal, so the measured speed collapsed and the fastest events were being rejected. Scoring speed over the build-up only raised agreement with a human-validated reference set from 62.6% to 94.4%.
  • Version 2 — 92.2% judged genuine, and frozen. Added the corrected speed test, a straightness test on the build-up, and a requirement that the build-up actually contain fills rather than a carried-forward flat line.

Two residual failure families are recorded rather than tuned away: small events in wallets that oscillate constantly, and events whose peak sits hours after the fast move. Neither is fixable by moving a threshold.

B2. Parameters we settled on

ParameterChosenWhy this value
Size of movez ≥ 6 Specified as 8, lowered after measuring that a trailing scale runs ~1.8× a full-sample scale precisely at event times — so trailing z = 6 is already stricter than the earlier study's full-sample z = 8. At z = 8 the catalogue drops to 76 shocks and discards two-thirds of events a reviewer had already confirmed.
Minimum economic size$100k peak deviation The position must move at least $100,000 worth of HYPE away from its own baseline. Without a dollar rule, a wallet that normally sits perfectly still would qualify on a $2,000 wobble, because the test is relative to that wallet's own noise.

Is $100k a lot? It depends entirely on whose shock you are looking for.
• For these ten wallets, no: their median shock is $713k and each trades over $1m on a qualifying day. The rule almost never binds.
• For the wider MM population, yes, it is a high bar: the median market maker on the absorbing side of one of these events takes on about $27k–$32k of inventory. A $100k floor would classify most of them as unshocked by construction.
This is why the population analysis does not use this gate (see the note on peers below).
Suddenness60% of the move inside 25 minutes At least 60% of the position build must happen within a single 25-minute stretch of the build-up, so a slow drift does not count as a shock. Measured over the build-up only, not the whole window — scoring it over the whole window made the fastest events score worst, because any window containing the spike also contains the reversal.
Widening this to 30 minutes has been requested and is not applied: it re-runs detection and moves every count in this report, so everything here is the 25-minute catalogue.
Baseline6-hour rolling median Preferred over 12-hour: near-superset of its catalogue and finds 2.5× as many permanent steps, which are exactly the family this study exists to admit.
Local prominence1.5× nearby excursions The single most consequential threshold — it removes 520 of the 792 candidates reaching it. Raising it to 2.0 also removes events reviewers passed.
Scale floor$12,500 / price What it is for. A shock is "the position moved far more than this wallet's normal wiggle", so we divide the move by that wallet's normal wiggle. Some wallets are so steady that their measured wiggle is almost zero, and dividing by almost zero makes any tiny move look enormous. The floor says: never treat a wallet's normal wiggle as smaller than this dollar amount.

Why the value matters. The detector fires when the move is at least 6× the wiggle. So the floor quietly sets a minimum shock size of 6 × floor:
• floor $100,000 → 6 × $100,000 = $600,000 minimum shock, which overrides the $100k rule we actually chose, and deletes four of the ten wallets from the catalogue entirely.
• floor $12,500 → 6 × $12,500 = $75,000, which is below $100k, so the explicit $100k rule stays the binding one.
$12,500 is chosen so the floor does its one job — stop division by a near-zero wiggle — without secretly becoming a size rule.
Deliberate exclusion. This detector finds sudden changes. A wallet that moves a lot of inventory slowly and permanently registers zero shocks — one of the ten does exactly that. Zero shocks means "no sudden change", never "no inventory change".

C. What causes a shock

All cause-side measurement is over the formation window — median 10 minutes.

Measured over 181 shocksMedianReading
Hit-side taker volume vs its trailing 24h rate5.29× The side trading against the MM accelerates sharply
Shocks with any hit-side surge92.8%Nearly universal
Shocks with the surge above 2×82.9%Not a marginal effect
Taker imbalance toward the hit side+0.443 Flow is one-sided in 87.8% of shocks
Direction split125 up / 56 down Takers sell into these MMs 2.2× as often as they buy

A shock is a burst, not a regime. Measured in detail on three episodes, the hit side surges roughly twice as hard as total volume (6.4× / 27.3× / 60.3× against 3.7× / 14.0× / 34.3×), while the opposite side also rises 2.1–15.4×. So both sides accelerate; the hit side accelerates far more, and imbalance jumps about tenfold above its trailing median. Reporting only total volume would miss the mechanism; reporting only the hit side would overstate one-sidedness.

D. Who else was there

Detection runs on ten wallets, but the question "who absorbed this" is only meaningful against everyone who was quoting. All of section D compares against every wallet labeled a HYPE market maker on the shock's UTC date: over the 181 shocks that is a median of 249 labeled wallets (p25 220, p75 262; range 102 to 374), of which a median 95 clear the pre-event activity gate (p25 77, p75 118; range 37 to 237).

Why the denominator decides the answer. Measured across the ten wallets only, the shocked wallet holds 60–77% of same-side inventory movement. Measured against every active MM, the largest single MM holds 23–36% and the ten together 36–47%. "It absorbed this alone" is what a ten-wallet denominator looks like, not what the market did.

D1. Absorbing a shock versus keeping it

Two questions on one set of fills: how widely was the burst spread across market makers, and how much of what each MM took was it still holding when the shock peaked? Both are measured on the same fills, over the same window, in the same unit — HYPE — so the gross and the net figures reconcile exactly and dividing one by the other is meaningful.

Who counts as a market maker mm_population/data/label_spine.parquet, rows with coin = hype and is_mm true on the shock's date. one wallet × date

Shown except the raw hhi_ columns, which carry no extra information — eff_n = 1/hhi.

Not shown because the check passed exactly: the median absolute residual is 0.0000 of gross acquisition, which is why ladder rows 4 and 5 agree to 0.01.

shock_wallet_absorb_retain.csv — 13,925 rows × 16 columns. user, peak_utc, wallet, acq, disp, acq_maker_hit, acq_taker, disp_maker, acq_maker_hit_legacy, acq_legacy, net_legacy, net, dq_grid, recon, retention, is_focal. All quantities are sizes in HYPE. disp_maker, acq_legacy and net_legacy are diagnostics and appear nowhere in D1.

One further table sits behind section D but not behind D1's numbers: tables/shock_absorption_allmm.csv (181 × 56) is the earlier population block, deliberately not rebuilt so it stays the record of the published numbers. The "shocked peers" count below and the dollar splits in Figure 6 come from it; every eff N and retention figure in D1 does not.

Full derivation, the validation run and the revision history are in analysis.md §13.1, which is the authoritative record.

The window: which fills count, and what the “legacy window” in row 0 is

A wallet's position is stamped at the end of each five-minute bin: the level on bin b is its position after the last fill in [b, b+5m). So the inventory change pos[t1] − pos[t0] is produced by the fills in [t0+5m, t1+5m) — the aligned window, and the window every primary number in D1 uses. The first version of the absorption measure instead summed fills in (t0, t1], one bin earlier: that is the legacy window. It survives only as row 0 of the ladder, so the size of the mistake is a measured quantity rather than an assumption.

Worked example. A shock forming from 12:00 to 12:10 has an aligned window of 12:05–12:15 and a legacy window of 12:00–12:10 — they share one bin out of two. A shock that forms in a single bin, 12:00 to 12:05, has an aligned window of 12:05–12:10 and a legacy window of 12:00–12:05: no fill is in both. The median formation window is 10 minutes and the p25 is 5, so a quarter of the catalogue was in that second case. Across the 181 shocks the shift moves the absorber count by a median of 4 wallets (p95 35) and eff N by a median of 1.46 (p95 8.6).

Maker size, taker size, gross, net

Every fill carries a crossed flag, so each wallet's HYPE splits two ways. The shock side is the direction the shocked wallet's inventory moved: on an up shock, buying HYPE.

Maker size on the shock side — acq_maker_hit
HYPE bought on the shock side on a resting quote: the wallet was standing there and a taker crossed into it. This is absorbing — supplying the liquidity the burst consumed — and it is the numerator of every absorption share.
All size on the shock side — acq
The same, plus size the MM went out and bought by crossing the spread itself (acq_taker). For the median absorbing wallet that adds nothing — its taker share of gross acquisition is 0% — which is what makes ladder row 2 a near-null step.
Sold back — disp
Size traded against the shock side in the same window: the MM unloading what it just took.
Net still held at the peak — net = acq − disp
What the MM was actually carrying at t1. Positive means still leaning with the shock. Gross versus net is the one comparison D1 exists to make — same wallet, same fills, same unit.
Grid position change — dq_grid
pos[t1] − pos[t0], signed to the shock, read off the five-minute position panel instead of summed from fills. Carried only to show it reproduces net — it does, to a median residual of 0.

The four populations, and how many wallets each is

These four counts get confused with each other constantly, so each is named with its own denominator. The counts vary by shock — a quiet Sunday and the October crash are not the same market — so each is given as p25 / median / p75 over the 181 shocks, with the range.

Active MMs — 77 / 95 / 118  37 to 237
Wallets labeled a HYPE market maker that date and past the activity gate before the shock: at least 10 grouped fills, and volume at or above the date's p10 among wallets clearing that count, in the two hours before the window opens. This is eligibility measured before the event — it says nothing about what the wallet then did. Column n_active_mm.
Absorbers — 58 / 71 / 92  17 to 231
Of those active MMs, the ones with at least one maker fill on the shock side. If takers are selling into bids, an absorber is any MM whose resting bid got hit at least once. The denominator of every absorption share. Column n_absorbers.
Same-side wallets — 51 / 63 / 80  11 to 213
Of the active MMs, those whose net position change over the window went the same direction as the shock. Selected by outcome, not by behaviour — and the shocked wallet passes this filter by construction, so the filter can only remove other wallets and raise the shocked wallet's share. Column n_l4_net_active.
Shocked peers — 1 / 4 / 12  0 to 68
Of the active MMs, those whose net change was both same-side and at least 3σ on their own scale: the MMs that took an abnormal hit, not merely a same-direction one. Column n_peers_comoved in shock_absorption_allmm.csv; it feeds D2, not the ladder below.
The shocked wallet ("focal")
The one wallet of record whose shock this row is — one of the ten detected wallets (9 appear in this catalogue). It is a member of every population above. Wherever a "share" is quoted below, it is this wallet's share of that row's total.
"Effective number" is not a count of wallets. With HHI = Σ share² over a participant set, eff N = 1/HHI is the number of equal-sized participants that would produce the same HHI. "Eff N = 11.3 across 71 absorbers" means: the 71 wallets' shock-side buying was as concentrated as if 11 equal MMs had split all of it and the other 60 had done nothing. One wallet taking everything gives 1; ten wallets at 10% each give 10; one wallet at 50% plus fifty at 1% gives 3.8, not 51. Because it is an index over a specific participant set, it cannot be compared across two different sets.
The ladder: six counting choices, one change at a time (reference — how 11.3 vs 7.4 was established)

Each row changes exactly one thing from the row above, so each difference is attributable to that one change. How to read the columns:

  • What is counted, per wallet — the HYPE quantity summed for each wallet before any concentration is computed. The column name in shock_absorb_retain.csv follows it.
  • Over which wallets — the eligible set the shares are taken within. Only two sets appear: the absorbers and all active MMs.
  • Wallets: eligible → counted — median size of that eligible set, and of those, how many had a positive amount of this row's quantity. The second number drops when the quantity is netted, because an MM that sold back everything it took contributes zero. This is why row 4 says "all 95 active MMs" and still counts 63.
  • eff N — over the 181 shocks, the p5 / p25 / median / p75 / p95 of the per-shock effective number. Lower means more concentrated.
  • Shocked wallet's share — median over the 181 shocks of the focal wallet's own share of that row's total.

Row 0's eligible set has no single count because the legacy window changes which wallets qualify as absorbers at all; 65 is the median that did. Rows 4 and 5 measure the same thing two ways — from fills and from the position panel — and agreeing is the point.

Each eff_n_* column in shock_absorb_retain.csv, one line each (every quantile column in the table is the p5 / p25 / median / p75 / p95 of that per-shock value across the 181 shocks):

  • eff_n_l0_absorb_maker_legacy — effective number over absorbers' gross shock-side maker size, on the superseded one-bin-early window; kept only as the bridge to the previously published number.
  • eff_n_l1_absorb_maker_P — the same on the aligned window [t0, t1] (window start → peak): gross maker size bought on the shock side, over absorbers. The headline gross concentration.
  • eff_n_l2_absorb_all_P — adds taker fills: gross size acquired on the shock side, maker + taker, same absorbers.
  • eff_n_l3_net_P — net size still held at the peak (acq − disp), same absorbers. The headline net concentration.
  • eff_n_l4_net_active — the same net quantity with the eligible set widened to all active MMs.
  • eff_n_l5_dqgrid_active — the position-panel change pos[t1] − pos[t0] instead of summed fills, all active MMs; its agreement with row 4 is the cross-check.

What this says

  • The whole gap is round-tripping. Same wallets, same fills, same unit: gross shock-side buying is as concentrated as 11.3 equal MMs, what those MMs were still holding at the peak as concentrated as 7.4, and the move is in that direction in 96% of shocks — a per-shock ratio of 1.47 (p5 0.96, p25 1.20, p75 1.79, p95 3.08), above 1 in 93% of shocks. Widening the eligible set moves eff N by −0.02 and switching to the grid position change by +0.01, so neither of those was doing any work in the old comparison.
  • When is "keeping" measured? Two senses, two times. Everything in this subsection is measured at the shock peak — the end of the build-up, a median 10 minutes after the window opens — so it is within-build-up pass-through: of the size bought while the takers were hitting, how much was already traded back before the peak. Keeping in the post-shock sense — how much of the excursion is still held τ after the peak, relative to the excursion itself — is §E1's remaining shock fraction (Figure 7): the shocked wallet of record still holds a median 12% of its excursion at peak+2h and 3% at peak+6h (p25–p75 at +6h: −28% to +35%); over every shocked MM in the population the median is 59% at +2h and 38% at +6h, and for shocked MMs outside the ten it is 75% and 56%.
  • Within the build-up, absorbing MMs pass a median 43 of every 100 HYPE straight back, keeping 57 at the peak. Retention = net size still held at the peak ÷ gross size bought on the shock side over the same window — HYPE over HYPE, same wallet, so it cannot exceed 1 and 0 of 10,937 values do. Aggregate per shock: p5 0.20, p25 0.44, median 0.57, p75 0.74, p95 0.85 (quantiles across the 181 shocks). In the median shock the absorbers buy 248,700 HYPE ($9.86m at the peak mid) on the shock side and are still holding 145,100 HYPE ($5.61m) at the peak. The ratio is null for a wallet that bought under 100 HYPE (about $4k at a $40 mid, where one 10-HYPE fill would swing it by 0.1): that floor drops 2,988 of the 13,925 wallet-rows carrying a median 0.22% of gross acquisition.
  • At the peak, pass-through and warehousing are two populations, not one average. Per wallet, 25% of absorbing MMs had already passed back 90% or more of what they took by the peak and 37% still held 90% or more (pooled per-wallet retention p5 −0.23, p25 0.10, median 0.68, p75 1.00, p95 1.00). Retention at the peak also falls with size taken (Spearman −0.16 over 10,937 wallet-rows): median 0.82 in the smallest size quintile against 0.44 in the largest.
  • At the peak, the shocked wallet holds modestly more of what it bought than comparable MMs: about 11 more HYPE per 100. It is the 97.8th percentile of absorbers by size, so the peer set has to be size-matched or the comparison repeats the original error. Against size-matched peers (gross within 2×, else the 5 nearest in log size) its peak retention is +0.112 higher — median paired difference, 63% of shocks positive, Wilcoxon p = 3e‑08; against the size-weighted peer average, +0.186; against the plain peer median, +0.062. That is why its share of the leftover position (15.0%) exceeds its share of the take (8.6%) — as a per-shock ratio 1.19, not 2. Note the contrast with the post-shock numbers above: the wallet that holds more at the peak is also the one that is flat soonest afterwards.

D2. Are the shocked MMs shocked on the same side

EpisodeActive MMsShocked On event sideOpposite Lift vs merely active
2025-08-11, up9113100%0+23.1 pp
2025-08-22, down741492.9%1+3.7 pp
2025-10-10, down (crash)1364175.6%10+18.3 pp
  • Shocked MMs are almost always on the event side — 100% / 93% / 76% across the three episodes, versus 57–89% of active MMs merely leaning that way: a shock selects the side, it does not just amplify a common drift.
  • The crash day is materially weaker — 10 of 41 shocked MMs were shocked the other way, which is what a two-sided cascade looks like from the maker side, and a reason not to pool that day with normal conditions.
  • Only 14–23% of active MMs are shocked at all, against 57–89% merely leaning the same way. "Everyone leaned, a minority took a real hit" is the accurate summary.

D3. Do they trade with each other

"MMs unload onto each other" needs three questions answered in order: (1) do shocked MMs take at all — cross the spread — and how does their taking change from before the peak to after it; (2) do they take more than they usually do, in the direction that reduces the shock — direction matters, because taking that adds to the position is a different act from taking that unwinds it; (3) only then, is the wallet on the other side another MM more often than usual. What exists so far is a slice of (3) for three episodes — the counterparty shares below, measured from exact taker–maker pairing, not inferred from timing — with no before/after split and no baseline for "more than usual". Questions (1) and (2), and the baseline for (3), are queued in the follow-up plan. Until then this table reads as a description of where MM taker flow went during formation, not as evidence of unloading onto peers.

MM→MM share of MM maker volume16.2%46.5%19.1%
Shocked wallets' maker volume filled by an MM taker8.8%56.5%17.1%
Shocked-to-shocked volume$0.08m$0.08m$2.10m
  • When an MM crosses the spread during these events, a fifth to two-thirds of that volume is taken from another MM's quote.
  • The first two rows are not comparable with each other: they share a numerator (MM→MM volume) over denominators of different size — MM taker volume is $4.20m / $2.63m / $28.3m against maker volume of $10.6m / $3.63m / $30.9m — so the taker share is arithmetically larger wherever MMs take less than they make. Read each row against its own denominator only.
  • Shocked wallets trading with each other is negligible in normal conditions but $2.10m on the crash day — under stress they do unload into each other. Consistent with both "unloading onto peers" and "peers were simply the resting liquidity"; the data does not separate those.

How the roster ten behave in one detailed episode

E2. The price

Measured over a fixed 60 minutes after each wallet's peak, on the shock-reducing side only, against every wallet trading that side in the same window off the same reference price. A fixed window is required so a fast wallet and a slow wallet are not compared over different spans. In the table below, Shocked MM and MM peers are each a median taken across shocks, while Gap is the median of the per-shock paired difference. Gap is therefore not the difference of the two columns beside it, and it is the paired figure that is like for like.

MetricShocked MMMM peers GapPercentile among peers
Price vs own peak mid (bps)+16.2+18.3−0.448.0
M30 (bps)−7.6−8.8−1.046.5
M60 (bps)−15.3−10.7−1.048.9
Taker share of reducing fills0.010.00+0.0163.7
  • The shocked MM gets the same prices as every other MM trading that direction at that moment. Like for like the gap is 0.4 bp on price and 1.0 bp on both markouts, at the 46th to 49th percentile of peers: a coin flip.
  • A negative markout is the normal condition, not a symptom. The shocked wallet's 60-minute markout of −15.3 bps sits against a peer median of −10.7 bps: losing money on reducing fills over the next hour is what that side of that window paid everybody.
  • Speed does not buy worse execution. Wallets that got flat printed much worse absolute prices than wallets that sat still (−76.9 vs +14.1 bps against the peak mid), but benchmarked, that difference is when they traded relative to the price path, not how well.
  • Unwinding is a post-only activity. The median taker share of reducing fills is about zero across the whole shocked population — the concession is in where quotes sit, not in crossing the spread. Shocked MMs do cross slightly more than peers (92% of shocks), but at tiny levels.
Order types used to unwind

Across 181 shocks the ten detected wallets unwind with post-only limit orders (84.4% of volume on average, 97.9% median) and immediate-or-cancel orders (14.3% average) — together 98.7%. Not once with a scheduled time-weighted order or a frontend market order. Two wallets are exceptions and cross the spread routinely: one for 80% of its unwind volume, another for 20%.

One wallet's event in full detail

F. What this does not establish

  • No causality. All associations are on a five-minute grid. A flow burst coinciding with an inventory build is not a demonstrated cause.
  • Shocks are detected on ten wallets only. Events where only other MMs were shocked are invisible, and there are no shock counts or rates for MMs outside the ten. Every population figure here is measured inside a window those ten wallets defined.
  • Most shocked MMs are outside the detected set — 9 of 13, 10 of 13 and 26 of 31 in the three detailed episodes — so the ten are not a representative sample of who gets hit.
  • Slow permanent re-targeting is out of scope by construction. The detector requires suddenness; it keeps only 18.5% of a comparable study's slow durable level changes.
  • Detector precision is 92.2%, not 100%. Errors concentrate in small events in noisy wallets.
  • Quoting behaviour is only observed where quotes were filled. No order-lifecycle data, so no claim about posted quote distance, quoted size, or a wallet's own bid-ask spread. A maker buy-versus-sell price gap is a realized fill-conditional gap, never a quoted spread.
  • Counts are wallet-concentrated. Two of the ten wallets account for 99 of 181 shocks; three contribute 6 between them. Any per-wallet cell below about ten events is indicative only.
  • Small samples in the detailed sections. The side-agreement, counterparty and speed-versus-price results rest on 13–41 shocked wallets per episode and 20 wallet-events in the speed split.
  • Position data has a known defect. About 12% of five-minute position changes in the underlying panel are not fully explained by visible fills. Detected shocks are essentially unaffected, but the defect constrains any looser variant.
  • A feed inconsistency affects 3 of 181 shocks, where maker volume on the absorbing side exceeds the taker volume it should match. Those rows are flagged and all shares use maker volume as the denominator.
  • Counterparty pairing is unavailable after 2025-11-24, so section D3 cannot be extended across the full window.
  • 2025-10-10 is a distinct regime — 41% of its formation flow is forced liquidation or auto-deleveraging, and markout magnitudes are an order of magnitude larger. It is labeled throughout and must not be pooled.

Full derivations, every table, and the complete revision history are in analysis.md, which is the authoritative record; this report is a reading of it.

G. Figure gallery

Every figure behind sections B and C at full size: one sampled page of audited shock panels, then the sixteen episode-pilot figures for the three episodes studied at one-minute resolution. Shared conventions throughout — times are UTC, buys green and sells red, maker versus taker shown by marker fill or hatching and never by colour, and a gold band marks the formation window in every time panel.

How to read these panels — the panel key, once, for all sixteen

An episode from the market side (six panels on a one-minute UTC axis, from 2 h before t0 to at least 4 h after t1; the gold band is the union formation window). (1) HYPE trade-price candles with a dashed vertical at each member's peak. (2) Whole-market taker volume, $k per minute, buys up and sells down, the forced part (liquidation + ADL) hatched black; dotted horizontals are the trailing-6 h median per-minute rates. (3) Rolling five-minute taker imbalance, (buy−sell)/total. (4) Median strict-pre spread per minute, bps. (5) Each roster MM's inventory change since t0 in kHYPE, shocked wallets coloured by rank and the rest grey. (6) Five-minute deviation z-scores with the ±3 loose and ±6 detector lines.

One member in detail (five panels, same time axis). (1) Price candles with that wallet's own fills overlaid: buy ^ / sell v, maker hollow / taker filled, marker area proportional to √(fill USD). (2) Its one-minute fill-anchored inventory in kHYPE against the trailing 6 h median (grey dash), formation leg shaded orange, red dot at the deviation peak — placed at the end of the peak five-minute bin, because positions are end-of-bin levels. (3) Maker-fill distance from the strict-pre mid (filled circles) and from its own-side best quote (open squares), per-minute volume-weighted, bps, positive = passive; the grey line is the median half-spread, so fills below it improved on the touch. (4) Own fill volume, $k/min by side, taker hatched. (5) Cumulative M5/M30/M60 markouts on shock-reducing fills after the peak, $k, with the unwind summary printed above.

An unwind overlay. X is minutes since each wallet's own peak on a five-minute grid; Y is remaining shock fraction, sign·(position − pre-median)/amplitude — 1 at the peak, 0 fully recovered, above 1 if the position kept moving, below 0 on overshoot. One line per shocked wallet coloured by rank, wallets that met only the looser 3σ bar dashed, dots at time-to-half (y = 0.5) and time-to-back (y = 0.25).
